Trip info

✨ Highlights▾
  • Alberobello: over 1,500 trulli, UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996
  • Matera: cave Sassi and the Palombaro Lungo, a 15-meter cistern carved beneath the main square
  • Taranto: the Ori di Taranto at MArTA, gold jewelry from the 4th to the 1st century BC
  • Gravina in Puglia: a 90-meter aqueduct bridge spanning the canyon
☀️ Weather▾

Best period: April-June and September-October, 18-27°C, dry air. Avoid July-August, when inland Murge temperatures often exceed 35°C and the ravines become impassable in the afternoon. Winter stays mild on the coast but colder and windier at 400 meters, in the Valle d'Itria.

📋 Notes▾

An entirely road-based loop: no leg exceeds 40 minutes of driving, and the route returns to Bari airport. The cave churches at Mottola, the Cripta del Peccato Originale at Matera, and the crypt of San Biagio can only be visited with advance booking.

A 13-day loop departing from Bari, through 46 stops across Puglia with a foray into Matera. The route strings together the Adriatic coast, the Valle d'Itria with its trulli, the white hilltop towns of northern Salento, then the ravines of the Ionian arc and the Alta Murgia. Everything is done by car; no leg exceeds 40 minutes of driving.

Stop 1 of 46
Bari

Bari

★★★☆☆
1

One crypt alone is worth the detour: the one beneath the Basilica di San Nicola in Bari. Saint Nicholas's relics arrived here on May 9, 1087, brought from Myra by Barian sailors in what was a very deliberate act of pious theft. The basilica, built between 1087 and 1197, now serves as a shared house of worship: Catholic mass upstairs, Orthodox liturgy in the crypt. Come early in the morning, before the pilgrim groups arrive.

⏱ 60 min
2

Dedicated to a 6th-century bishop, the Cathedral of San Sabino lives in the shadow of its neighbor San Nicola, which is exactly what makes it worth visiting. Beneath the nave, the succorpo opens onto Roman streets, frescoes, and the remains of a Byzantine cathedral: a city beneath the city. Allow 60 to 75 minutes including the crypt. Tourist access closes during services, so check times before heading in.

⏱ 70 min
3

The Castello Normanno-Svevo closes off the old town on the western side, moat included. Founded around 1131 under Roger II and reworked by Frederick II around 1233, it has changed purpose with every century: fortress, residence, today offices and exhibition halls. The Gipsoteca displays plaster casts of sculptures from across the region, strangely moving. Entry around 8 euros, including a section of Bari Sotterranea.

⏱ 60 min
4

White limestone bounces light across Piazza Mercantile and Piazza del Ferrarese, the two open-air drawing rooms of Bari Vecchia. One faces the port, the other acts as a transition between the medieval city and the 19th-century Murattian district, laid out on a grid. The terraces fill instantly at the start of the evening: get there before 8pm or forget about a good view.

⏱ 40 min
5

Small museum, big subject: the Museo Nicolaiano, opened in February 2010, tells the story of how sixty-two Barian sailors went to Myra to retrieve the relics of Saint Nicholas. Liturgical objects, parchments, silverware donated by pilgrims. An hour is enough, and it sits right next to the basilica, no detour needed. Opening hours shift by season, check the day before.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Head down Strada Arco Basso around 10am, when the women of Bari Vecchia are shaping orecchiette at their doorsteps with a knife stroke that takes years to master. It's thoroughly touristy and utterly genuine at the same time: they sell to neighbors and curious visitors alike. A bag costs a few euros. Ask before photographing someone's face; most of the time, they'll say yes.

⏱ 45 min

If you have an evening in Bari, check the program at the Teatro Petruzzelli, one of the city's three historic theaters alongside the Margherita and the Piccinni. Opera, concerts, ballet: seats go fast and the hall is worth the ticket even for a middling program. The other two venues also have schedules, often at lower prices.

Polignano A Mare

★★★★☆
1

Lama Monachile lives up to its reputation: a pebble cove wedged between two cliffs at the mouth of an ancient stream bed carved through limestone. The name is said to derive from the monk seals that once frequented these caves. The Bourbon bridge arching above it, some fifteen meters high, dates from the early 19th century. In August the beach is packed by 9am: come at sunrise or resign yourself to standing.

⏱ 45 min
2

Built in the 13th century and consecrated around 1500, the Chiesa Matrice Santa Maria Assunta faces Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II, known locally as the Clock Square because of the neighboring Casa dell'Orologio, which once housed the university. Apulian Romanesque on the outside, reworked within. Polignano's historic center has no great monument to tick off: it's a backdrop, not a museum. Step in, then step back out and wander.

⏱ 30 min
3

The locals simply call them the poems: the verses painted on steps, doors, and walls throughout the historic center are the work of Guido Lupori, known as Guido il Flâneur, who started in 1984. Even the Mark Twain quote on one wall is his, and Twain never set foot here. Look for them by lifting your eyes; most visitors walk right past.

⏱ 40 min
4

A three-meter bronze figure with arms flung wide, which sounds excessive, and yet the statue of Domenico Modugno works. The singer of Nel blu dipinto di blu, better known as Volare, was born here in 1928; Hermann Mejer's sculpture shows him facing the Adriatic, jacket catching the wind. It stands on the seafront promenade that bears his name, two minutes from Lama Monachile. Queues for photos form in the late afternoon.

⏱ 20 min
5

The Museo Pino Pascali on Lungomare Cristoforo Colombo is the contemporary art stop nobody expects to find in Polignano. The museum is named after an Apulian artist and also hosts temporary exhibitions. It's small, air-conditioned, and quiet when the town is heaving: the right move during the hot hours, between 2pm and 5pm.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Touristy, but the only real way to see Polignano: a boat trip along the sea caves that pierce the cliff face, including the famous Grotta Palazzese, home to the cliff-side restaurant. From the water, you understand why the white houses seem to float in midair. Departures from the harbor in late afternoon for the best light. Rough seas mean cancellation, so build in a backup plan.

⏱ 60 min

The caffè speciale smells of almond and cream before it even reaches you: it's Polignano's specialty, served at the counter in bars throughout the center. Another local curiosity is the carota di Polignano, a Slow Food Presidium since 2013, worth tasting raw from market stalls. And yes, the octopus sandwich at Pescaria is worth the queue, just not at 1pm.

Monopoli

★★★☆☆
1

Built in the 16th century to ward off Turkish raids, the Castello di Carlo V did its job: the town was never taken. Its irregular pentagonal layout even encompasses an ancient Basilian church, San Nicola della Pinna. It served as a prison until the 1950s. Not everything is accessible, as part of it houses municipal offices, but the view from the bastions over the Porto Vecchio is more than worth it.

⏱ 45 min
2

The Cattedrale Maria Santissima della Madia tells the story of a raft. In 1117, tradition holds, a boat loaded with timber arrived in the harbor, carrying an icon of the Madonna, and the wood was used to finish the church roof. Some of the beams are preserved as relics. The present building is an 18th-century Baroque reworking with polychrome marble and gilding. Every December 16, the scene is reenacted in a procession on the sea.

⏱ 45 min
3

Blue on white: the fishing boats of Monopoli's Porto Vecchio stand out against the ramparts. This isn't a set piece; the fishermen still go out, mostly for octopus. The best vantage point for photos is from the jetty facing the castle, boats in the foreground. Just after sunset, the lights reflect on the water and the basin changes completely.

⏱ 30 min
4

Get lost between Piazza Garibaldi, Piazza Palmieri, and Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II: Monopoli's historic center threads through narrow alleys that suddenly open onto these broad squares. The contrast is the whole point. Notice the white loggia of Palazzo Martinelli along the way, 18th century, almost Venetian in feel. Put the map away; the old town is too small to get truly lost.

⏱ 60 min
5

If Baroque churches interest you, Monopoli's Museo Diocesano completes the cathedral, just a few steps from Largo Cattedrale. The territory also has cliff-face cave churches carved into the coastal cliffs, far less visited than the center. Museum hours are reduced off-season; call ahead before making the trip.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

The best swimming in town isn't at Capitolo but at Cala Porta Vecchia, right at the foot of the ramparts: you jump in the water from the historic center itself. It's small and fills fast. The Capitolo beaches further south are wider but cost money and are packed in August. Arrive before 10am for Cala Porta Vecchia.

⏱ 90 min

The locals call it a sporcamuss, literally dirty-mouth: a puff pastry soaked in custard and dusted with icing sugar, physically impossible to eat neatly. The name is a warning, not a metaphor. You'll find it in pastry shops throughout the center, best eaten warm. Bring a napkin, seriously.

Conversano

★★★☆☆
1

The Castello di Conversano occupies the high point of the former acropolis, a Norman fortress that became the home of the Acquaviva d'Aragona counts. Inside, the Pinacoteca Paolo Finoglio displays ten canvases inspired by Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered. Entry around 5 euros. Climb to the terraces at sunset and the countryside spreads out all the way to the sea.

⏱ 60 min
2

Built between the 11th and 12th centuries, the Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta plays the Apulian Romanesque card fully: gabled facade, a 15th-century rose window, nothing superfluous. It can be spotted from the surrounding fields. Just steps away, the Galleria Cattedrale shows work by Apulian artists in a few rooms.

⏱ 30 min
3

A women's monastery that outranked the local clergy: the Monastero di San Benedetto earned its abbesses the nickname Monstrum Apuliae. In 1266, nuns replaced the Benedictine monks, and Pope Gregory X authorized the abbess to wear episcopal insignia. The bell tower stands taller than the cathedral's, and that was no accident. The civic archaeological museum now occupies the ground floor.

⏱ 45 min
4

The Chiesa di San Cosma e San Damiano, a few streets away, is worth stepping into: full Baroque, commissioned by Isabella Filomarino, one of the figures who funded art in Conversano. Plain outside, rich inside. Opening hours are erratic; try your luck in the morning.

⏱ 20 min

If you're passing through in May or June, stop at the market stalls: Conversano lives by its cherries, which colour the surrounding countryside at that time of year. The rest of the year it's orchards and dry-stone walls, with nothing to buy. Growers sell by the roadside, not at the covered market.

Castello Marchione

Grotte Di Castellana

★★★★★
1

The air drops to 16-18°C in an instant, seventy meters below the Murge plateau: the Grotte di Castellana open through the Grave, the only cavern connected naturally to the surface, 100 meters long, 50 wide, 60 deep. The opening of sky above you lingers for a moment, then disappears. Bring a light layer and flat-soled shoes, even in August.

⏱ 30 min
2

Pay for the full route, not the short one: the Grotta Bianca is only accessible on the 3km tour, roughly 100 minutes of walking. Near-translucent alabaster, walls that reflect the spotlights back at you. The partial route covers 1km in 50 minutes and stops before reaching it. Tickets sell out fast in summer; book online.

⏱ 100 min
3

The Museo Speleologico Franco Anelli, at the cave exit, is named after their discoverer. Scale models, exploration equipment, workshops for children: it's brief but puts the visit in perspective. The underground network extends far beyond the section open to the public. Ask at the ticket desk what's included in your ticket.

⏱ 40 min

Activities

If you're there on a summer evening, look out for the Speleonight: the tour runs in darkness, which changes everything, including the acoustics. Dates are limited and so are spots. Failing that, aim for the first slot of the morning, fewer crowds and a less rushed guide.

⏱ 120 min

Putignano

★★☆☆☆
1

A metal spiral staircase descends a dozen meters straight down, through the interior of a trullo: the Grotta del Trullo in Putignano demands commitment. Discovered on May 29, 1931 during sewer work, it was opened to visitors before the Castellana caves. Amber and ivory formations, a vertical cavity reaching 19 meters. Allow half an hour.

⏱ 30 min
2

Dating to the 12th century and consecrated around 1500, the Chiesa di Santa Maria la Greca holds the relic of Saint Stephen's skull, patron of the town, and a Byzantine icon of the Virgin. It's Putignano's oldest church. It often closes between noon and 4pm; schedule the visit for the morning.

⏱ 25 min
3

The Chiesa di San Pietro Apostolo dominates the main square of the historic center: a Romanesque structure from the 13th-14th centuries, interior redone in Baroque style, imposing facade. This is Putignano's mother church, and the contrast between the outside and inside sums the town up rather well. A few minutes inside, then back into the white alleyways.

⏱ 20 min
4

Book ahead before visiting the Palazzo del Balì, home of the Casa Museo Guglielmo Romanazzi Carducci: built in the 14th century for the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem, later a residence of the Romanazzi-Carducci princes. Entry announced at 6 euros for adults, 4 euros for ages 7 to 25. Visits by appointment, not open access.

⏱ 45 min

Alberobello in e-bike. Trulli, countryside, mill and donkeys

★ 5from 47 €

Explore trulli and nature with your personal fitness coach

★ 5from 15 €

Activities

The local mascot is called Farinella, like the dish: a flour of roasted barley and chickpeas, served with sughi, cime di rapa, or fava bean purée. Putignano's carnival, one of Italy's longest, claims more than 600 editions and parades with papier-mâché floats. A trail of photos and papier-mâché pieces is displayed throughout the historic center.

⏱ 60 min

Putignano artichokes are worth the detour in spring, green or purple depending on the variety, found at local markets rather than restaurants. Add the tarallini made with flour, olive oil, and white wine, and the intonchiata, an almond braid. The surrounding vineyards produce Primitivo and Malvasia.

Noci

★★★☆☆
1

Private courtyards that were once streets: the gnostre of Noci are former passageways, gradually enclosed as houses were built around them over the centuries. Today they're micro-squares where laundry dries and children play. No entrance fee, nothing to check off, that's the whole point. Walk through; no car fits in here.

⏱ 45 min
2

Founded in 1316 by Philip I of Anjou, who is said to have promised a chapel after sheltering under a walnut tree during a storm, the Chiesa Matrice Santa Maria della Natività gave the town its name. It preserves 14th-century baptismal fonts and a Madonna and Child attributed to Stefano da Putignano. Across the square, the Torre dell'Orologio, completed in the early 19th century.

⏱ 30 min
3

The Abbazia della Madonna della Scala, about 6km from Noci toward Gioia del Colle, is worth the drive out. Built in 1930 around an older church whose Romanesque doorway survives, it houses a community of Benedictine monks and a still-active workshop for restoring antique books. Silence expected; hours follow the monastic offices.

⏱ 40 min

Activities

If you're there in early November, Bacco nelle Gnostre fills these courtyards with new wine and roasted chestnuts on the first weekend of the month. It's one of the region's major vino novello events. The rest of the year, the gnostre host concerts and tastings.

⏱ 90 min

Noci is somewhere to eat more than to visit: the town has held the title of Città dell'Enogastronomia since 2005 and lives by its latticini, fresh mozzarella and burrata. The fornelli, butcher shops that cook meat on the premises, are the local institution. Come early on Sunday; the morning fiordilatte goes fast.

⏱ 60 min

Santa Maria Di Barsento

★★★★☆
1

The Chiesa di Santa Maria di Barsento stands alone in open countryside, a few kilometers from the town center. Built according to tradition in 591 at the request of Pope Gregory the Great, it has a basilical plan with a chiancarelle roof: the same technique used for trulli, roughly a thousand years before trulli. Checco Zalone filmed a baptism scene here. Dirt track at the end; wear proper shoes.

⏱ 30 min

Alberobello

★★★★☆
1

A thousand cones and souvenir shops everywhere: Rione Monti in Alberobello is saturated, and still astonishing. Around 1,030 trulli line its sloping alleyways, their whitewashed rooftops painted with symbols. The quarter is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 1996. Come before 9am or after 6pm; in between, the tour buses unload.

⏱ 75 min
2

Then cross into Rione Aia Piccola, where no commercial business may operate: that's the rule, and it holds. About 590 trulli, all inhabited, laundry at the windows, no one trying to sell you a fridge magnet. The contrast with Rione Monti, a hundred meters away, is absolute. Keep your voice down; people actually live here.

⏱ 45 min
3

Trullo Sovrano is the only two-story trullo in town, which is enough to make it a curiosity. Dating from the 18th century, it's set up as a house-museum with original furnishings from the early 20th century: the best place to understand how people lived under a cone. Entry announced at around 2 euros. Fifteen minutes is enough; it's tiny.

⏱ 20 min
4

A church shaped like a trullo: the idea could have been absurd, and somehow it isn't. The Chiesa di Sant'Antonio, at the top of Rione Monti, uses the same chiancarelle construction and blends into the quarter rather than overpowering it. It's the only church built this way. The climb is steep; save it for the end of the loop, when the light is falling.

⏱ 25 min
5

Two cones fused at the centre: the Trulli Siamesi owe their name to this shared roofline. Local legend sees two brothers, a story of love and hatred, and a house divided in two. They line Rione Monti, steps from the shops. Five minutes, long enough to study the joint between the two cones.

⏱ 10 min
6

Find Casa d'Amore at the entrance to the center: this is the first building constructed after Alberobello was freed from the fiscal obligations imposed by the King of Naples, in 1797. It served as the first town hall. Nothing extraordinary to look at, except that it marks the turning point in the town's entire history. Explanatory panel on site, two minutes.

⏱ 10 min
7

Locorotondo

★★★★☆
1

The pointed rooftops catch the light differently here than in Alberobello: in Locorotondo, they belong to the cummerse, white houses with pitched roofs covered in chiancarelle limestone slabs. The historic center is laid out in concentric rings, hence the name, locus rotundus. A one-hour walk covers it. Look for the Latin inscriptions carved into the lintels.

⏱ 60 min
2

A 16th-century facade and a 35-meter dome: the Chiesa Madre di San Giorgio dominates the central square, wildly out of proportion with the village. It's the landmark that brings you back to the center when you get turned around in the alleyways. Open mornings and late afternoons, closed at siesta.

⏱ 30 min
3

Locorotondo's lungomare has no sea: it's a panoramic road suspended above the Valle d'Itria, with views all the way to Martina Franca. Trulli, vineyards, and dry-stone walls as far as the eye goes. The name is a local joke, fully intended. Come in late afternoon when the valley turns golden.

⏱ 30 min
4

Make a point of walking past Palazzo Morelli at Via Morelli 30, dated 1819: carved doorway, family coat of arms, one of the finest examples of civil architecture in the village. It's a private residence, not a museum; you admire it from the street. Two minutes, then back into the alleyways.

⏱ 10 min
5

Porta Napoli marks the entrance to Locorotondo's historic center, with the town's coat of arms engraved in the ground. It opens onto Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II, the village's living room, formerly Piazza Castello. The Torre dell'Orologio rises above it, now housing the municipal historical archives. The best starting point for the walking loop.

⏱ 20 min
6

Find the Chiesetta di San Nicola di Myra, tucked into the white facades: from the outside, nothing sets it apart from the houses on either side. Built in 1660, it conceals a vault painted in its entirety, devoted to the life and miracles of the saint. It doesn't open every day; try in the morning, it's free and worth the detour.

Martina Franca

★★☆☆☆
1

Rebuilt from 1747 after the 1743 earthquake, the Basilica di San Martino is the high-water mark of Martinese Rococo. Its local limestone facade rises 37 meters, divided into two registers, with a high relief of the saint sharing his cloak. It stands on Piazza Plebiscito. Step inside: the contrast with the spare alleyways outside is jolting.

⏱ 45 min
2

Walk through the gate of Palazzo Ducale, today Martina Franca's town hall: built in 1668 on the foundations of a 1338 castle, it was intended to have 300 rooms, chapels, and a theater. It was never finished. The Piano Nobile rooms, Arcadia, Myth, and Bible, preserve 1776 frescoes by Domenico Carella and are open to the public.

⏱ 60 min
3

Piazza Plebiscito is the town's stage: the basilica on one side, the Palazzo dell'Università and the Torre Civica on the other, with its 1734 clock. Café terraces, evening passeggiata. Photograph it at sunset, when the local stone turns the colour of honey.

⏱ 30 min
4

The curved arcades of Piazza Maria Immacolata offer welcome shade in July: locals simply call it la Rotonda. Designed by Davide Conversano, they wrap around the square and the Fanelli, Caramia, and Marino Motolese palaces. It's the most photographed square in Martina Franca. A coffee under the arches at 6pm and you'll understand the town.

⏱ 30 min
5

Take Via Cavour, Via Garibaldi, or Via Mazzini for Martina Franca's noble palaces: wrought-iron balconies, Rococo doorways, Palazzo Torricella, Palazzo Nardelli, Palazzo Barnaba, Palazzo Stabile. The 17th and 18th centuries were the town's golden age and the families competed in facade-building. Best light early in the morning.

⏱ 45 min
6

The Chiostro di San Domenico is worth visiting even outside festival season: it's one of the outdoor performance venues in summer, and a silent cloister the rest of the year. The Chiesa di San Domenico completes Martina Franca's Baroque circuit. Check access; it depends on current events.

Egnazia

★★★★☆
1

Erected in the 4th century BC, the Messapian walls of Egnazia enclose an entire city left open to the sky, on the coast near Fasano. The first settlement dates to the 16th century BC and life continued here until the 13th century AD. Fifteen hectares of archaeological park, with not a tree in sight. Hat and water are non-negotiable; there is no shade anywhere.

⏱ 40 min
2

Walk the Via Traiana, the road Emperor Trajan had built between 108 and 110 AD to link Benevento to Brindisi, as an alternative to the Appian Way. At Egnazia, it separates the public buildings from the residential and craft quarters. The ruts worn by cart wheels are still visible in the stone. It's the best thread to follow through the site.

⏱ 30 min
3

The cryptoporticus is the best-preserved section of the Egnazia park, and you can walk through it entirely: a covered underground passage, cool and intact. Next to it, the Basilica Civile with its aula delle Tre Grazie, the shrine to eastern deities, the colonnaded square, and the baths. Allow two hours for the park alone.

⏱ 45 min
4

Pomegranates painted on the walls of a tomb: the Tomba delle Melagrane at Egnazia is a Messapian funerary chamber from the 4th century BC. The necropolis, outside the walls, lines up pit graves, semi-chamber tombs, and full rock-cut chambers, some decorated with frescoes. An aristocracy wealthy enough to commission underground rooms for its dead.

⏱ 30 min
5

The Museo Nazionale Giuseppe Andreassi completes the park across seven sections, from the 16th century BC to the 13th century AD when the site was abandoned. Eleven bright pavilions arranged around two courtyards. In the 19th century, the tombs were looted first by foreign officers and then by agricultural workers: much of the funerary furnishings is now scattered. Multilingual audio guides available.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Take a guided tour of the excavations and museum at Egnazia: without commentary, the site looks like a field of stones; with it, a city comes back to life. Systematic excavation campaigns started in 1912 and continue today. Extended hours from April to September, until 7:15pm. Book morning slots in summer.

The Torre Guaceto headland closes the reserve on the seaward side, and it's the only spot where the full sequence makes sense: fields and olive groves, then scrubland, then wetlands, then dunes, then the Adriatic. The Aragonese tower gives its name to the entire marine protected area. Some zones are closed to swimming to protect the habitat, and that's not for show. Read the signs before laying down your towel.

⏱ 45 min
2

Sand, dunes, nothing else: the Spiaggia delle Conchiglie is the main beach of Torre Guaceto, and a 2019 excavation campaign uncovered a Bronze Age necropolis here. People swim here in summer, directly above tombs three thousand years old. Private vehicles are prohibited up to the beach: shuttle or bicycle, no exceptions.

Mask, fins, snorkel: snorkeling at Torre Guaceto is done with marine biologists, above posidonia seagrass beds. Salema, mullet, sea urchins, sea turtles, a seabed left intact by protection. A triangular castle is rare enough to be worth a stop: the Castello Dentice di Frasso in Carovigno has one square tower, one round tower, and a third almond-shaped one, its point aimed toward the sea. 2

Piazza 'Nzegna is the heart of Carovigno, given its character by the convent complex of Maria Santissima del Monte Carmelo. Cafés, comings and goings, village life. 3

Dating from the 14th century, the Chiesa Madre di Santa Maria Assunta in Cielo anchors Carovigno's historic center, alongside the Chiesa di Sant'Angelo and the Chiesa del Carmine, known for its 18th-century frescoes. Three churches within a few hundred meters. Hours follow the service schedule; late morning is a good bet.

4

Follow the line of Carovigno's former town walls: four towers still mark the perimeter, Del Prete, Delli Brandi, Giranda, and Del Civile, some round, others square. Ostuni

★★★★☆
1

A Gothic cathedral in Puglia is almost an anomaly: the Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta in Ostuni was built between 1435 and 1495, when the region was building Romanesque or Baroque. Its central rose window has 24 petals. National monument since 1902. It occupies the highest point of the old town: the climb earns it, so go early.

⏱ 45 min
2

The Arco Scoppa spans the alleyway in front of Ostuni's cathedral, connecting the Palazzo Vescovile to the old seminary. Originally built in wood, it was reconstructed in stone in 1750 on the orders of Cardinal Scoppa. Locals simply call it la Loggia. It's the town's mandatory photograph: come before 9am if you want it without a crowd underneath.

⏱ 15 min
3

The locals call it la Terra: Ostuni's historic center was once whitewashed throughout, which is where the white city nickname comes from. Alleyways, hidden courtyards, medieval arches, staircases, all climbing the highest of three hills. Nothing to check off, everything to wander through. Flat shoes essential; the slopes are serious.

⏱ 90 min
4

A pregnant woman who died more than 25,000 years ago: Delia is preserved at the Museo di Civiltà Preclassiche della Murgia Meridionale, housed in Ostuni's former Carmelite monastery. She was found in a local cave, crouching, her foetus still in position. She's the single exhibit that justifies the ticket on its own. The museum is small; allow an hour.

⏱ 60 min
5

Opened in 2017, the Museo Diocesano di Ostuni occupies the Palazzo dell'Episcopio, right next to the cathedral: the Collezione Archeologica Capitolare alongside works from surrounding churches and monasteries. It also serves as a temporary exhibition space. Useful when the midday heat drives you off the alleyways at 2pm.

⏱ 45 min
6

Piazza della Libertà is Ostuni's main square at the foot of the old town: the Chiesa di San Francesco, the former Franciscan convent converted into the Palazzo di Città, and the guglia di Sant'Oronzo, the column dedicated to the town's patron. Everyone ends up here in the evening. Terraces fill from 7pm in summer.

⏱ 30 min
7

Walk the Aragonese walls of Ostuni for the view: the plain of olive trees runs all the way to the sea, eight kilometers away. Two ancient gates still stand, Porta Nova and Porta San Demetrio. This is the best place to understand why the town was built here and nowhere else. Late afternoon, when the light rakes across the olive groves.

San Vito Dei Normanni

★★☆☆☆
1

In 1943, King Victor Emmanuel III took refuge in Brindisi with Badoglio and set up here: the Castello Dentice di Frasso in San Vito dei Normanni housed the Italian head of state during the collapse. Its Norman tower from the 11th-12th centuries stacks three rooms; the rest was added from the 15th century onward. Decorated halls, paintings, hunting trophies, restored archives.

⏱ 45 min
2

The frescoes of the Cripta di San Biagio are captioned in Greek, save one: that of Saint Nicholas, which carries a Latin inscription. This Byzantine sanctuary is carved into the rock near the masseria Jannuzzo, with the monks' cells still visible, mixing Orthodox and Latin saints on the same walls. Access by reservation only; don't turn up unannounced.

⏱ 45 min
3

Built in 1571, the Basilica di Santa Maria della Vittoria is what the people of San Vito simply call the chiesa madre. It faces the center of town. Nothing spectacular, but it's the landmark that anchors everything else. Five minutes in passing.

⏱ 20 min
4

The Museo della Civiltà Rurale in the Chiostro dei Domenicani in San Vito dei Normanni is worth a visit: opened in 2001, it gathers the objects of an agriculture that disappeared within a generation. Tools, utensils, reconstructions. The cloister alone is worth the visit. Reduced hours; call ahead.

⏱ 40 min
5

Only discovered in 1985, the Castello di Alceste occupies the highest point in the San Vito dei Normanni territory, on a rise in the middle of open countryside. The name misleads: it's an archaeological site, not a castle. Nothing is set up for mass tourism, which is exactly the point. Ask in town about access before heading out there.

Mesagne

★★★☆☆
1

Robert Guiscard erected a castrum at Mesagne in 1062-63, and everything flows from there. The Castello Normanno-Svevo retains its tall quadrangular keep, with machicolations for dropping stones and boiling oil, four corner bartizans, a freshwater well, and underground dungeons. Destroyed in 1256 by Manfred's Saracens, it was rebuilt two centuries later. Municipal property since 1973.

⏱ 60 min
2

The MATER, Museo del Territorio Ugo Granafei, has occupied a wing of Mesagne's castle since 1999: Bronze Age vessels, Messapian and Roman material, medieval ceramics, a lapidarium, and a numismatic collection including Greek coins minted at Taranto, Metaponto, Sybaris, and Crotone. In the entrance hall, a former ice store, a half-chamber tomb has been reassembled. An hour is enough.

⏱ 60 min
3

Built between 1650 and 1660, the Cattedrale di Tutti i Santi dominates Piazza IV Novembre in the center of Mesagne. It's one of the most restrained examples of Baroque in Puglia, without the usual excess. It still serves as a reference point for locals arranging to meet. Open mornings and late in the day.

⏱ 30 min
4

Get lost in Mesagne's historic center, clustered around the castle: Palazzo del Cavaliere, the late-19th-century municipal theater, a string of churches including the Chiesa di Sant'Anna. Beneath the alleyways, the castle's cellars were used to store oil from the underground mills of the quarter. An hour-long loop, no hills.

1

The Castello Svevo d'Oria has a triangular layout, three towers, well-preserved walls, and an outsized parade ground. Frederick II was attached to this town, and the castle bears his name even though it's the product of centuries of reworking: the cylindrical Salto and Cavaliere towers were added in the Angevin period, gun ports cut in the 15th-16th centuries to absorb firearms. National monument, private property since 2007.

⏱ 60 min
2

Porta Taranto is also known as Porta degli Ebrei, and the name is not incidental: it opens onto the Judea, the medieval Jewish quarter of Oria, whose community settled here from the 9th century and made its mark in literary and scientific fields. A stone shield crowns the gate, its heraldry worn away. The quarter is a half-hour walk.

⏱ 40 min
3

Enter through Porta Manfredi to approach Oria's center in the right direction: medieval squares and alleyways, then the noble palaces, the Sedile, Palazzo Martini Carissimo, and Palazzo Vescovile. The town sits at 160 meters above sea level, on a hill between Brindisi and Taranto. Light colors and narrow streets do the rest.

⏱ 45 min
4

The Basilica Cattedrale of Oria houses the Cripta delle Mummie, and the name says most of what needs saying: it's one of the most unsettling visits in the area. It sits in the historic center, steps from the castle. Access to the crypt is restricted and hours change by season; call the parish rather than trusting third-party websites.

⏱ 40 min
5

The MAM, Museo Archeologico e dei Messapi Demetra e Persefone, occupies the Sedile and Palazzo Martini Carissimo in central Oria: objects found across the territory, from the Messapian world through the Roman period. The Museo Diocesano in Palazzo Vescovile completes the visit on the sacred side. Two small museums, an hour and a half between them.

⏱ 90 min

Activities

If your trip falls in early August, Oria steps back into the Middle Ages: the Corteo Storico di Federico II and the Torneo dei Rioni restage the tournament the emperor organized in 1225 for his wedding to Yolande of Brienne. Over 800 participants, four competing quarters: Castello, Judea, Lama, and Santo Basilio. The tradition has run continuously since 1967.

⏱ 180 min

Buy taralli messapici before leaving Oria: the town claims a recipe that tradition traces back to the Messapians, and you'll find them in bakeries throughout the historic center. Add orecchiette with cime di rapa, a dish eaten here every day rather than just for tourists. Bakeries close in the afternoon.

Francavilla Fontana

★★☆☆☆
1

Half fortress, half palace: the Castello Imperiali in Francavilla Fontana was built in 1450 by Giovanni Antonio del Balzo Orsini, Prince of Taranto, then reworked in the Baroque style in the 18th century. A four-arch loggia, sculptures, half-columns, battlements now purely decorative, moat filled in. Today it houses the town hall and the MAFF, the archaeological museum. Museum open weekends; check the time slots.

⏱ 60 min
2

The MAFF covers Francavilla Fontana and the Brindisi plain from the Palaeolithic to the modern era, with pieces also from Ceglie Messapica, Mesagne, and Brindisi. 3D reconstructions, illustrations, objects. It occupies the halls of the Castello Imperiali. Announced opening hours: Saturday and Sunday, 10am-1pm and 5pm-9pm: plan your visit for a weekend.

⏱ 60 min
3

Piazza Umberto I concentrates what Francavilla Fontana has that's most photogenic: its fountain, its arcades, and its clock tower, more than twenty meters tall. It's the town's meeting point, with the bars under the arches. Nearby, Porta del Carmine, the oldest gate in the city, where public executions were once carried out.

⏱ 30 min
4

Eleven meters tall, twenty in diameter: the Specchia Miano sits hidden in the olive trees a few kilometers from Francavilla Fontana, on the road to Ceglie Messapica. Nobody knows exactly what these pre-Roman Messapian structures were for, watchtowers or funerary monuments. This one is among the best preserved. Dirt track at the end; a car with low clearance isn't advised.

⏱ 30 min

Activities

The mandorla riccia is eaten in Francavilla Fontana and nowhere else: an almond cake recognized as a Traditional Agri-Food Product of Puglia, produced exclusively here. Pastry shops in the center make it all year round. Add the taralli, cavatelli, and ricotta-filled ravioli if you stay for lunch. It keeps several days if you're taking some home.

Ceglie Messapica

★★☆☆☆
1

The Castello Ducale dominates Ceglie Messapica from its hill, and its Norman tower on the left is what survives of the 11th-century original. The rest alternates expansions and abandonments across almost a thousand years. The municipality has recovered and restored a section, now open to visitors. Enter through a wide doorway. Views over the surrounding countryside.

⏱ 45 min
2

A cast of a Middle Palaeolithic hyena den: the MAAC, Museo Archeologico e dell'Arte Contemporanea installed in the Castello Ducale of Ceglie Messapica, does nothing the conventional way. It also contains a Hellenistic funerary monument and the furnishings of local Messapian burials. The complex houses the Pietro Gatti library and the Emilio Notte art gallery. Allow an hour.

⏱ 60 min
3

Ceglie Messapica was called Kailia under Greek influence, around 2,700 years ago, and was wealthy enough to become a Messapian military capital. Four defensive circuits protected the town across a perimeter of about five kilometers. Where the Chiesa di San Rocco now stands, tradition holds there were once two temples dedicated to Apollo and Venus. Explore the historic center on foot.

Take the old road between Francavilla Fontana and Ceglie Messapica by bicycle if possible: it passes through rural contrade and connects a series of specchie, these pre-Roman megalithic towers. The Specchia Giovannella is actually a Hellenistic tower, built with perfectly squared interlocking blocks and no mortar. The word comes from the Latin specula, meaning to observe. Rocky tracks; mountain bike recommended.

Grottaglie

★★★☆☆
1

The smell of wet clay hits you before the alleyways do: the Quartiere delle Ceramiche in Grottaglie clings to the gravina di San Giorgio, with workshops and kilns carved directly into the rock. In dialect they're called li Camenn're, the chimneys. You reach them by steps, along the walls of the Castello Episcopio. Come in the morning, when the ceramicists are at the wheel.

⏱ 90 min
2

A symbol of the feudal power of the bishops of Taranto, the Castello Episcopio raises its 14th-century square tower over the historic center. It houses the Museo della Ceramica, which traces the evolution of local production century by century. Courtyard, halls, panoramic terrace. In the evening, lit up from the ceramics quarter, it's worth looking at from below too.

⏱ 60 min
3

The Collegiata Maria Santissima Annunziata is Grottaglie's chiesa madre, at the top of the historic center, steps from the castle. It's the classic starting point for guided tours of the town, before heading down to the workshops. Quick, but it puts everything else in context. Fifteen minutes.

⏱ 20 min
4

The Chiesa del Carmine in Grottaglie houses a cave crypt dedicated to the Madonna della Grotta, with an adjoining convent. On the way, spot the ceramic pumi placed on balconies, those stylized buds said to bring good luck, and the Cappella dei Santi Pietro e Paolo. Palazzo Pignatelli is visible from the street.

The Gravina di Riggio is the most impressive of the ravines encircling Grottaglie, and a waterfall runs at its floor. Allow half a day if you're descending into Riggio, and wear shoes that grip.

⏱ 120 min
6

Street art murals in the middle of a ceramics town: Grottaglie opened its walls to street artists, often in the most unexpected corners of the historic center. Taranto

★★★☆☆
1

The Ori di Taranto fit into a handful of display cases and justify the journey: gold jewelry crafted between the 4th and 1st centuries BC, excavated throughout the region. The MArTA, Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Taranto, on Via Cavour, covers everything else from the Palaeolithic to the Middle Ages, including the statue of Zis, a Messapian deity. Open daily, long hours. Minimum two hours.

⏱ 120 min
2

The Castello Aragonese locks off the entrance to Mar Piccolo with its pentagonal footprint. First Byzantine nucleus around 780 AD, then Ferdinand II of Aragon had it reworked in the late 15th century by Francesco di Giorgio Martini, military engineer. Today it belongs to the Italian Navy and is open to visit free of charge, guide included. Book ahead: slots are limited despite the free entry.

⏱ 90 min
3

Two columns still standing, and that's all that remains: the Doric temple in Piazza Castello, Taranto, is described as the oldest place of worship in Magna Graecia. It's embedded today in the convent of San Michele, now a music institute. The square also concentrates the Palazzo di Città and the Castello Aragonese. No admission, just look.

⏱ 30 min
4

Founded around the mid-10th century, the Duomo di San Cataldo is considered the oldest cathedral in Puglia. Its facade was redone in the 18th century; inside, a dome with Byzantine overtones sits alongside Baroque excess, and the saint's relics are in the chapel at the back. It stands on Piazza Duomo in the heart of the Città Vecchia. Smart dress required.

⏱ 45 min
5

Taranto's Città Vecchia occupies an island between two seas, and it hasn't been repainted for postcards: tired facades, drying laundry, craft workshops, Baroque churches at street corners. It's the oldest and most lived-in quarter of the city. Belvedere at Piazza Fontana at sunset. In the evening, stay on the well-frequented main streets.

⏱ 90 min
6

The Ponte Girevole connects the old town to the new by pivoting on itself, above the canal joining Mar Grande and Mar Piccolo. The canal was dug in 1481 against the Turks; the first bridge dates from 1887, operated by a hydraulic system fed from a cistern in the castle. The current electric version has been running since 1958. Watch it open; it's the city's signature spectacle.

⏱ 30 min
7

The Chiostro di San Domenico completes the Città Vecchia loop in Taranto, with the Chiesa di San Domenico Maggiore and the Chiesa del Carmine. Taranto has many centuries-old convents and cloisters, and they're the quietest spots on the island. Twenty minutes each, fitted in between alleyways.

⏱ 40 min

Legend has it that Taras founded the city on a dolphin's back, and dolphins are still here: the Jonian Dolphin Conservation takes visitors out on observation trips in the Gulf of Taranto alongside researchers. This isn't a dressed-up tourist cruise; it's data collection. Reservation required, trips cancelled in rough weather.

⏱ 240 min

On May 8, Taranto sends its saint to sea: the statue of San Cataldo is loaded onto a boat and followed by a flotilla in procession, and as it enters the canal the castle releases a cascade of fireworks. This is the city's feast day, not a tourist reenactment. Out of season, it's a reason to plan a May visit.

Massafra

★★★☆☆
1

A Baroque staircase descends to the Santuario della Madonna della Scala, set at the bottom of Massafra's ravine. The building dates from 1731, constructed over an earlier chapel, and the Virgin is depicted here with two does at her feet, hence her other name, Madonna della Cerva. Pope Pius VI named her patron of the city in 1776. Descend in the morning; the climb back up is in full sun.

⏱ 60 min
2

An 11th-century pharmacy carved into the tufa, inaccessible to visitors: the Farmacia del Mago Greguro in Massafra lines up twelve interconnected caves carved high into the cliff face, riddled with a hundred regular niches. Legend places a healer and his daughter Margheritella here around the year 1000; archaeologists see instead an old monastery converted into a pigeon house. You look at it from below.

⏱ 30 min
3

The Grotta del Ciclope opens at the base of the ravine wall in Massafra, its name drawn from the Odyssey rather than archaeology. Given its size and large platform, it looks more like an agora, a meeting place for the cave village; the presence of a kiln also suggests craft use. It's on the descent path. Uneven ground; closed shoes.

⏱ 30 min
4

On the sanctuary forecourt, the Cripta della Madonna della Buona Nuova preserves outstanding cave paintings, including a Virgin of the Good News and a Christ Pantocrator with Deesis. Part of it was demolished in the 19th century to enlarge the forecourt, which tells you something about the period. Massafra has around thirty cave churches of this type on its territory.

⏱ 30 min
5

The Gravina di San Marco cuts Massafra in two, and three viaducts stitch the town back together: the Ponte degli Zingari, the Ponte Nuovo, and the Ponte Vecchio. It's the attraction nobody expects on arrival: a gorge running through the center of a town. The Parco Naturale Regionale Terra delle Gravine encompasses the whole area. Cross the bridges on foot to grasp the depth.

⏱ 40 min
6

Pasolini filmed his Gospel According to St. Matthew here, and the historic center of Massafra still goes by the nickname Pasolini's Capernaum: mazes of whitewashed alleys, underground chambers, castle. The town is also known as the terra dei masciàri, the land of sorcerers. The ravine floor, covered in medicinal plants, is called the Valle delle Rose.

It's nicknamed the Sistine Chapel of cave art, and the comparison holds up: the chiesa rupestre di San Nicola at Casalrotto, near Mottola, is carved into tufa, three naves, an iconostasis in the Byzantine style, a cycle of frescoes restored in 1972. A cave church arranged on two levels of circulation: the chiesa di Sant'Angelo is embedded in the cave village of Casalrotto, on the territory of Mottola. It hides in a valley that lacks the scale of the great ravines, which is exactly why people walk past it without seeing it. A guide is essential to find it.

Around a hundred caves carved on both sides of the ravine: the villaggio rupestre di Casalrotto, below Mottola, is reached by an old tratturo, a transhumance track. Castellaneta

★★★☆☆
1

One hundred and forty-five meters deep, three hundred wide: the Gravina di Castellaneta is a canyon carved by the Lato torrent, and the town sits right on its edge, perched at the brink. Several viewpoints in the historic center look directly into it. The walls are riddled with caves where Greek monks, and later peasants fleeing pirates, took refuge. The railing is low; keep children close.

⏱ 45 min
2

Rodolfo Valentino was born here in 1895, and Castellaneta has never let that go: the Museo Documentario Rodolfo Valentino has occupied the former Santa Chiara monastery since June 2010. Thirty-five film posters, screenings, previously unseen photographs, and a recreation of the set of The Son of the Sheik. Allow an hour.

⏱ 60 min
3

Castellaneta's historic center strings together light-colored noble palaces, carved doorways, and shops around the Cathedral, the Chiesa di San Domenico, and the Palazzo Vescovile. All of it sits on a plateau suspended above the ravine. You go from alleyways to the void in three steps. The Convento delle Clarisse is on Via Vittorio Emanuele.

⏱ 45 min
4

A majolica statue of the Sheikh at the end of a shopping street: it's the monument to Rodolfo Valentino, made in 1961, at the end of the Castellaneta promenade on Via Roma. On the same axis, a plaque marks his birthplace. He attended primary school here before Taranto, then America. In the evening, this is where everyone walks.

Matera

★★★★★
1

The Sasso Barisano is the larger of Matera's two cave quarters, and the most restored: hotels, restaurants, and workshops have taken over the former cave dwellings. You descend from Piazza Vittorio Veneto, then follow Via Bruno Buozzi. It's the logical entry point into the Sassi. Three to four hours for a complete loop of both Sassi, without rushing.

⏱ 90 min
2

The Sasso Caveoso preserves Matera's rawest caves: less restored, closer to what life looked like here before the 20th-century evacuations. Accessed from the Cathedral, you exit via Via Ridola toward the Piano. Piazza San Pietro Caveoso is its center. The paving stones are uneven and slippery in wet weather.

⏱ 90 min
3

A family, a donkey, and chickens all in the same room: the Casa Grotta di Vico Solitario reconstructs life in the Sassi of Matera in the 1950s, with original furniture and objects. Entry announced at around 3 euros. It's the visit that makes everything else in the city legible. Fifteen minutes, and you'll never look at the Sassi the same way again.

⏱ 20 min
4

Under Matera's main square lies a cistern the size of a nave: the Palombaro Lungo, built in 1864 as the water reserve for the Sasso Caveoso. The guided tour descends about 17 meters; the basin itself is 15 meters deep, linked to a network of caves and conduits. Entry announced at around 3 euros, hourly tours, beneath Piazza Vittorio Veneto.

⏱ 40 min
5

Santa Maria de Idris is carved into the rocky spur overlooking the Sasso Caveoso, and this is where the widest view across Matera is taken. The neighboring chapel of San Giovanni in Monterrone connects to it. Next door, the church of San Pietro Caveoso, on the square of the same name. Entry 2 to 4 euros per cave church; hours vary.

⏱ 40 min
6

The Civita quarter occupies the spur separating Matera's two Sassi, and the Cattedrale di Santa Maria della Bruna holds the highest point in the city. Romanesque, carved facade, a stark contrast with the surrounding caves. The view over the valleys makes the climb worthwhile on its own. Appropriate dress required to enter.

⏱ 45 min
7

San Pietro Barisano is the largest of Matera's cave churches, on the main route through the Sasso Barisano, Via Bruno Buozzi. It has a literal underground history: beneath the nave, decomposition chambers were used to prepare the bodies of clergy. Entry 2 to 4 euros. Check hours; they change by season.

⏱ 30 min
8

Casa Noha isn't just another cave house: it's a multimedia trail through the history of Matera's Sassi, including the part nobody likes to tell, the forced evacuation of the 1950s. Around 7 euros, open daily 10am to 7pm. Do this first, before descending: everything else you see afterward becomes clearer.

⏱ 40 min
9

Palazzo Lanfranchi, Piazza Giovanni Pascoli, closes off the Piano at the belvedere end and houses the city's art museum. The terrace in front offers one of the classic views over the Sasso Caveoso. Pascoli wrote that Matera was the city that smiled at him most. It's the best place to end the day, just before the sun goes down.

Add orecchiette with hand-made cime di rapa, and you have lunch sorted. The best batches come out early in the morning.

⏱ 40 min
3

Made an episcopal seat in the 9th century under the Byzantines, Gravina in Puglia passed to the Normans after 1040 and gained a Latin-rite cathedral: the Basilica Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta, built from the 11th to the 16th century. It dominates the historic center, with the Biblioteca Capitolare Finia alongside. Open mornings and late afternoons.

⏱ 40 min
4

Descend into the Fondovito and Piaggio quarters, the two medieval districts of Gravina in Puglia clinging to the canyon flank: cave dwellings, rock cellars, crypts. This is the core of what guides call the cave habitat, and it's inhabited, not museified. The terrace on Via Fontana La Stella gives the best viewpoint.

⏱ 60 min
5

The Fondazione Museo Ettore Pomarici Santomasi preserves the cripta di San Vito Vecchio, a Byzantine fresco crypt relocated inside the museum: the frescoes were removed and reinstalled, which saved them. The rest of the circuit covers the archaeology and art of the Gravina in Puglia territory. An hour and a half.

⏱ 90 min
6

Frederick II came to Gravina in Puglia for hunting, calling it his urbs opulenta and preferring it to his other hunting lodges, and he had a castle built here. The remains are outside the center, in the countryside. Nothing monumental to see, but it places the town within the geography of Swabian power. Dirt track at the end.

⏱ 40 min

Activities

If you're there in late April, the Fiera di San Giorgio takes over Gravina in Puglia from the 20th to the 25th: an ancient fair, definitely not a tourist market. The town regularly serves as a film location for Italian and foreign productions. Accommodation is hard to find on those dates.

Botromagno

★★★☆☆
1

The Botromagno archaeological zone and the cave crypt of the Padre Eterno are on the outskirts of Gravina in Puglia, and together they hold the oldest layers of the city. The Sette Camere hypogeal complex completes the series, with the pre-Christian temple turned into the Madonna della Stella. This is a territory, not a checklist: allow half a day.

Altamura

★★☆☆☆
1

Two stone lions flank the doorway and support the columns: the Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta in Altamura was begun in 1232 on the orders of Frederick II, and is one of the four palatine churches of Puglia. Apulian Romanesque in its original form, with later reworkings. It faces Piazza Duomo. The matronei galleries can be visited; ask at the entrance.

⏱ 45 min
2

Here they're called claustri: the small enclosed squares of Altamura's historic center, inherited from the Middle Ages, reached through narrow passages called strictuli. The center is ringed by megalithic walls that predate Frederick II's city by far. And everywhere, the smell of bread baking in stone ovens. A one-hour walking loop, with no effort.

⏱ 60 min
3

A complete Neanderthal skeleton still embedded in the rock: the Uomo di Altamura was found in 1993 in the Lamalunga cave, with estimates dating it between 130,000 and 300,000 years ago, depending on the source. The Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Altamura devotes a multimedia section to it, and covers the rest of the territory from the Palaeolithic to the Middle Ages. Two hours.

⏱ 90 min
4

The Centro visite Uomo di Altamura, near the masseria Ragone, lets you observe the skeleton virtually, as it remains in its cave: the remains have never been removed from Lamalunga and are not visible in person. Locals call him Ciccillo. It's the only way to see the specimen other than in photographs. Opening is calendar-based; call ahead.

⏱ 60 min
5

The chiesa di San Nicolò dei Greci in Altamura's historic center repays a brief visit: the name tells the story. Frederick II repopulated his city in 1230 with Latins, Greeks, and Jews, each with their own place of worship. It's a quiet witness to deliberate urban planning. Five minutes, on the claustri route.

⏱ 20 min

Thick crust, yellow crumb, keeps for several days. Ask to see the oven; most bakers say yes. Morning batches.

Pulo Di Altamura

★★★★☆
1

The Pulo di Altamura is one of the largest sinkholes in Puglia, a karst collapse in open countryside north of the city. The area has been inhabited since the final centuries of the Neolithic, as the surrounding excavations have amply demonstrated. This is a landscape, not a monument. Closed shoes; dirt paths.

Gioia Del Colle

★★★☆☆
1

The Castello Normanno-Svevo in Gioia del Colle escaped the military reworkings that disfigured other Apulian fortresses, which makes it the most faithful witness to the Norman and Swabian periods. Its north wing dates to the 9th-century Byzantine presence; Frederick II had it rebuilt around 1230. Rectangular plan, interior courtyard, two of the original four towers still standing.

⏱ 60 min
2

The throne in the Sala del Trono is a fake: it was assembled in 1907 during restoration, using carved fragments recovered from the castle after demolitions. Architect Angelo Pantaleo reconstructed by hand the staircase, the triforas, and this throne. The Sala del Camino next door retains an authentic Renaissance fireplace. National monument since the 1950s.

⏱ 40 min
3

Installed in the castle since 1977, the Museo Nazionale Archeologico in Gioia del Colle turns on a single question: what was life like in an ancient Apulian city? Peucetian vessels and objects from the 7th to the 3rd century BC, organized thematically: house and work, roles and functions, ideology. The circuit runs across two levels of the castle.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

The castle in Gioia del Colle has served regularly as a film set: Pasolini filmed Salome's dance for The Gospel According to St. Matthew here, and Matteo Garrone shot a scene of Tale of Tales in the throne room. Local legend has it that Manfred was born here and places the ghost of Bianca Lancia in the Torre dell'Imperatrice. Other sources locate the story at Monte Sant'Angelo.

Acquaviva Delle Fonti

★★☆☆☆
1

Four palatine basilicas in Puglia, and one of them is here: the Cattedrale di Sant'Eustachio in Acquaviva delle Fonti, alongside San Nicola in Bari, the cathedral of Altamura, and that of Monte Sant'Angelo. Started in 1529 by the dukes of Atri, finished in 1594, consecrated only in 1823. It takes the Romanesque plan of Bari and Bitonto and pushes it toward the Renaissance: rare in the region.

⏱ 45 min
2

The historic center of Acquaviva delle Fonti clusters around Piazza Vittorio Emanuele, where the cathedral opens. The town takes its name from the water table running beneath it, and its origins stretch back to the 7th century BC. The painter Carlo Rosa, of the southern Caravaggesque tradition, was born here in 1613. Half an hour's walk is enough.

⏱ 30 min

The cipolla rossa of Acquaviva delle Fonti is a Slow Food Presidium, and the municipality hosts a second one, the cece nero della Murgia carsica: two presidia on one territory, which is unusual. At table, ask for the calzone di cipolle, a flatbread stuffed with onions, ricotta forte, and cheese. Eat it warm, never cold.

⏱ 60 min

The WWF Gioacchino Carone oasis, a few kilometers from Acquaviva delle Fonti, is a detour worth taking: two and a half hectares of woodland, dense birdlife including the lesser kestrel. It's small, but it's what remains of the Murge's original forest cover. Access and visits managed by the WWF; check before heading out.

Casamassima

★★☆☆☆
1

A blue village in a region that paints everything white: the historic center of Casamassima is a maze of alleyways, arches, and chiassi, those dead-end passages, where the lime has been tinted azure. The tradition attributes this to a vow to the Madonna against the plague, in the mid-17th century. The color has faded, but the effect remains. Come in late afternoon, when the light catches it.

⏱ 60 min
2

The Porta dell'Orologio is the scenic entrance to the Casamassima village, built in the 19th century to replace the medieval gate. It opens from Piazza Aldo Moro, where the chiesa del Purgatorio, built around 1700, also stands. It's the starting point on foot and the town's symbol. Park on the square.

⏱ 20 min
3

Under the arch of Via Santa Chiara in Casamassima, a 17th-century fresco depicts the Madonna di Costantinopoli: it's from the colour of her mantle that Duke Vaaz is said to have drawn the village's blue, in gratitude for the end of the epidemic. A less romantic version holds that housewives reused blue-tinted washing water to whitewash the walls. Choose your story.

⏱ 15 min
4

Founded in 1573 by Antonio Acquaviva d'Aragona with his sister Dorotea's money, the Monastero di Santa Chiara is the most imposing building in Casamassima's historic center. Built as an orphanage, it became a Clarisses monastery a century later, then after Italian unification, a prison, school, cinema-theatre, and housing. Few buildings have accumulated this many lives.

⏱ 30 min
5

The Chiesa Matrice di Santa Croce in Casamassima was built over a 12th-13th-century church, and its courses of polished, regular blocks speak to the care of the original construction. It's in the old town, with the Palazzo Ducale a few steps away. Hours follow the services.

⏱ 25 min
6

The Polish Military Cemetery in Casamassima has nothing to do with the rest of the visit, and that's exactly why you should stop: it holds the Polish soldiers who fell during the Second World War. Silence, rows of graves, dates. A reminder that these hills witnessed more than harvests.

⏱ 30 min

Activities

Schedule your stop in Casamassima for the end of the day: the blue walls only work in raking light; at noon they disappear. The Balcone Fiorito festival animates the village with exhibitions, concerts, and markets, and includes a cena azzurra, a picnic that's entirely blue, tablecloths included. Dates published by the municipality.

⏱ 60 min

Bitonto

★★★☆☆
1

A griffin in mosaic beneath a cathedral: the Concattedrale of Bitonto was built over an Early Christian church, whose crypt preserves an 11th-century opus sectile pavement, remarkably intact. Lion's body, eagle's head, symbolizing the dual nature of Christ. The building, inspired by San Nicola in Bari, is regarded as the finest example of Apulian Romanesque.

⏱ 60 min
2

Look at the central doorway of the Cattedrale di Bitonto before entering: its narrative sculpture has no equivalent in Apulian Romanesque. Above it, a sixteen-petalled rose window, topped by a relieving arch with a sphinx, flanked by two lions on suspended columnettes. The portico planned in front was never built. Piazza Cattedrale.

⏱ 30 min
3

The Torrione Angioino guards the entrance to Bitonto's medieval quarter, near Porta Baresana: this is where all guided visits begin, and it's the right way to read the city. Bitonto was a Roman municipium, then Lombard, Byzantine, Norman, and Swabian: no period of rule missed the appointment here. Walking loop from the gate.

⏱ 30 min
4

Palazzo Sylos Calò is the civic showpiece of Bitonto: a 15th-century triple portico and a 16th-century loggia, around Piazza del Sedile, where churches, museums, and noble palaces line up. This is the square the town gathered in, literally. Twenty minutes, looking up.

⏱ 30 min
5

The Lama Balice rings Bitonto: it's the bed of the former Tiflis torrent, now a nature park, and the reason the town was defensible. Trails, vegetation, and the contrast with the olive groves covering the surrounding territory. Bring water; there are no facilities on the route.

⏱ 90 min

Activities

Bitonto's olive oil comes from the local Ogliarola di Bitonto variety, on groves that cover the territory to the horizon: the mills welcome tastings and explain production. The town also has its frantoi ipogei, underground olive mills carved beneath the historic center. The Galà dell'Olio marks the local calendar.

⏱ 90 min

Bari

★★★☆☆
1

The Murattian district is the exact opposite of Bari Vecchia: straight streets, laid out on a grid in the 19th century, shop fronts, and bourgeois buildings. Via Sparano is its main artery, pedestrianized, leading to the city's three theaters, the Petruzzelli, the Margherita, and the Piccinni. This is where the Bariotes take their evening passeggiata, not in the old town.

⏱ 60 min
2

The Chiesa di Santa Scolastica in Bari is no longer a church: it's the city's archaeology center and art gallery, installed within its walls. It overlooks the seafront at the tip of the old town. Few visitors make it up here, which is reason enough. Check hours; they depend on current exhibitions.

⏱ 60 min
3

The Fortino Sant'Antonio watches the sea from the other end of Bari Vecchia, opposite the Castello Svevo, and is systematically ignored by the tourist circuit. A discreet outpost, now used as an exhibition space. The view over the Adriatic and the old harbor is worth a ten-minute detour. Free entry according to current exhibitions.

⏱ 30 min
4

Walk the full length of Bari's lungomare before leaving: it's the city's meeting point, stretching between the fortino and the Murattian district, with fishermen, old men on benches, and the sea breeze. Nothing to visit, everything to take in. Late afternoon is best; the sun is harsh on this orientation in the morning.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Keep two hours before Bari airport: Via Sparano concentrates the shops, and the pastry shops in the Murattian district sell edible souvenirs worth taking home. Karol Wojtyła Airport is about twenty minutes from the center by car, and the loop closes where it began, at the Basilica di San Nicola.
